outputs.L1:
This original text is Geoffrey Chaucer’s famous 14th-century Middle English poem, ***Truth*** (also known as *Balade de Bon Conseyl*). 

Since Middle English can be difficult for modern readers to understand, below are two polished, professional versions in modern English: **Option 1** translates the text into eloquent, refined modern prose, while **Option 2** retains the poetic structure and rhythm.

---

### Option 1: Eloquent Modern Prose (Recommended for Clarity and Tone)

Flee from the crowd and live in truth; be content with what you have, however modest it may be. For hoarding breeds hatred, high ambition is precarious, the crowd fosters envy, and wealth blinds us all. Desire no more than what you truly need. Learn to govern yourself well before you attempt to advise others, and truth shall set you free—of that there is no doubt.

Do not distress yourself trying to correct every earthly injustice, placing your trust in Fortune, who rolls unpredictably like a ball. Great contentment lies in a simple, quiet life; beware, therefore, of kicking against the sharp points of fate, and do not fight as a clay pot does against a stone wall. Subdue yourself, you who are quick to judge the deeds of others, and truth shall set you free—of that there is no doubt.

Accept with humble grace whatever is bestowed upon you; struggling for worldly status only guarantees a fall. This world is not your home; it is merely a wilderness. Forward, pilgrim, forward! Step forth, creature, out of your stall! Know your true homeland; look up, and give thanks to God for all things. Keep to the high road, and let your spirit lead you, and truth shall set you free—of that there is no doubt.

Therefore, cast aside your former wretchedness and cease being a slave to the world. Ask mercy of Him who, in His supreme goodness, created you from nothing. Draw near to Him, and pray for heavenly rewards—both for yourself and for others—and truth shall set you free; of that there is no doubt.

---

### Option 2: Refined Modern Verse (Preserves Poetic Structure)

Flee from the crowd and dwell in truthfulness;  
Be satisfied with little, though it be small.  
For hoarding breeds hatred, and ambition instability;  
The crowd brings envy, and wealth blinds us all.  
Desire no more than what suffices for your call;  
Rule yourself well, if you would advise another’s deed,  
And truth shall set you free, you need not dread.  

Torment yourself not all wrongs to redress,  
In trust of Fortune, who turns like a ball.  
Great peace resides in modest busyness;  
Beware of kicking sharp points, lest you fall,  
Strive not like a clay pot against a stone wall.  
Master yourself, who judge what others do, indeed,  
And truth shall set you free, you need not dread.  

What you are sent, receive in humble grace;  
Wrestling for this world brings but a fall.  
Here is no home, but a wild, desert place;  
Forward, pilgrim! Step forth from your stall!  
Know your true home! Look up! Thank God for all!  
Keep to the high road, let the spirit lead,  
And truth shall set you free, you need not dread.  

Therefore, abandon your old wretchedness;  
Cease to the world to be a bounden thrall.  
Ask mercy of Him who, in His goodness,  
Made you from nothing; and in general,  
Draw unto Him, and pray for heavenly reward instead,  
For yourself and others; and truth shall set you free, indeed.

# The Way of Peace and Truth

In a world driven by constant noise, endless desire, and the relentless pursuit of status, the human soul often loses its way. We are conditioned to measure success by what we accumulate and control, yet true fulfillment lies in a radically different direction. To find lasting peace, one must turn away from the distractions of the world and embark on an intentional, inward journey toward truth.

True wisdom begins when we reevaluate our relationship with material things. Rather than chasing worldly ambition and the endless accumulation of wealth—which offer only a fleeting illusion of security—we ought to seek truth and remain content with modest means. A simple life clears away the clutter of greed and envy, creating space for the spirit to breathe. When we are satisfied with little, we are no longer slaves to the anxieties of loss and competition, finding a quiet richness in the unadorned reality of existence.

This simplicity of living naturally extends to our inner focus. It is far too easy to look outward, lamenting the injustices of the world or casting harsh judgment upon the flaws of others. Yet, exhausting one’s energy in a futile attempt to reform the entire external world often leads only to bitterness. The true battleground lies within. Our primary duty is to focus on mastering and correcting ourselves—governing our own passions, aligning our thoughts with virtue, and practicing self-discipline. True righteousness is not demonstrated by judging our neighbors, but by quietly transforming our own hearts.

To master oneself also requires a shift in how we respond to the tides of fate. We must learn to accept whatever life brings with genuine humility. The world is inherently fickle, and its fortunes shift without warning; to struggle fiercely against its unpredictable nature is to invite inevitable sorrow and a heavy fall. By surrendering our pride and receiving both trial and triumph with grace, we cultivate a quiet resilience. Acceptance is not passive resignation, but the wise acknowledgment that we are not the masters of the universe.

Ultimately, this peaceful endurance is made possible by a shift in perspective: viewing our earthly existence not as a permanent residence, but as a temporary pilgrimage. We are merely travelers passing through a realm of impermanence. When we stop clinging to the world as if it were our final destination, we allow our spirit to awaken. Guided by this higher awareness, our steps are naturally directed away from earthly distractions and toward our true, heavenly home.

In the end, ultimate freedom and deliverance are not achieved by conquering the world, but by relinquishing our attachment to it. By releasing our grip on worldly ambition and choosing to live in humble devotion to God’s truth, the soul breaks free from the chains of anxiety, fear, and desire. In this divine surrender, we finally discover the unshakeable liberty and eternal peace we were created to enjoy.

# The Freedom of the Wayfarer: On Contentment, Truth, and the Divine Journey

### I. The Illusion of the Market and the Crowd
To look upon the ceaseless bustle of the world is to observe a quiet tragedy played out on a grand stage. Humanity, driven by an unquenchable thirst for distinction, relentlessly pursues two deceptive masters: temporal wealth and public status. Yet, the rewards of this chase are bitter. The pursuit of riches inevitably breeds envy—a corrosive poison that rots the heart from within, forcing a person to measure their own worth solely by the possessions of their neighbor. 

Simultaneously, the craving for status binds the soul to the fickle whims of the crowd. Public favor is as unstable as the shifting sands; those who are praised today are discarded tomorrow. In striving to satisfy these insatiable appetites, individuals willingly enter into a form of spiritual bondage. They become prisoners of their own desires, chained to anxieties, fears of loss, and the endless demand to project an image of success. In trying to possess the world, they find that the world has, in truth, possessed them.

### II. The Sanctuary of Quietude and Virtue
To break free from this gilded cage, one must cultivate the courage to step away from the noise. Deliverance begins with a deliberate retreat from the crowd—not necessarily a physical flight into the wilderness, but an inward withdrawal from the madness of societal competition. In the stillness of solitude, the soul learns to breathe again.

Here, in the quiet, the practice of self-control takes root. Temperance is not the denial of life, but the mastery of it. By disciplining our impulses, we strip away the excess that weighs us down and learn the rare art of modest contentment. True abundance is not found in having much, but in needing little. When a person is content with simple, honest provisions, the threat of poverty loses its sting, and the allure of luxury loses its power.

To live in contentment is to live in truth. It requires shedding the masks worn for public applause and standing plainly as one is, grounded in integrity and moral clarity. 

### III. Truth as the Great Liberator
Ultimately, it is the adherence to truth that delivers the spirit from earthly suffering. Much of human anguish stems from living a lie—from believing that material things can bring lasting peace, or that human approval can confer ultimate value. When we embrace the truth of our condition, the illusions shatter. 

Truth reveals that suffering, loss, and the transience of worldly fortunes cannot diminish the integrity of a soul aligned with the Divine. By abandoning the false promises of the temporal world, we achieve genuine freedom. This freedom is not the license to do as one pleases, but the liberation from the frantic tyranny of appetite and ambition.

### IV. The Pilgrimage Home
To sustain this freedom, we must adopt a profound shift in perspective: we must realize that this life is not a permanent dwelling, but a temporary pilgrimage toward God. We are wayfarers passing through a foreign land. A wise traveler does not weigh themselves down with heavy, useless baggage that impedes their progress; they carry only what is essential for the road.

When we view our days through the lens of eternity, temporal desires naturally lose their hold on us. The trial of life becomes manageable, the gains and losses of the world turn insignificant, and the path ahead becomes clear. Eternal salvation is not merely a distant promise for the afterlife, but a present reality that begins the moment we untether our hearts from the earth and fix our eyes on the Creator. In recognizing God as our ultimate destination, we find at last the rest, stability, and joy that the world could never give.

In the heart of an ancient, whisper-thin forest lived a quiet, restless spirit named **Fle**. As the first harsh winds of autumn began to sweep across the northern ridges, it became clear that the time had come **for** a great journey toward warmer lands. 

Fle traveled light, carrying only the memory of summer’s warmth and a small brass lantern to guide the way through the twilight. Other creatures of the woods urged Fle to gather heavy stores of food and thick cloaks, warning of the long, unforgiving nights ahead. 

Yet, Fle smiled and shook their head. Experience had taught the little wanderer a simple truth: excess only slows the traveler down. A quiet clearing, a modest flame, and a moment of rest would always **suffise** to restore one's strength.

**For** miles, the path stretched through shadowy glades and over frosty peaks. Yet, with every step, Fle found that true comfort was never found in abundance, but in the freedom to move forward and the quiet peace of having just enough.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please provide the complete original Middle English text of Geoffrey Chaucer's poem "Truth" (also known as "Balade de Bon Conseyl").
counterfactuals.output:
Here is the complete original Middle English text of Geoffrey Chaucer's poem **"Truth"** (also known as *Balade de Bon Conseyl*), based on standard manuscript editions such as *The Riverside Chaucer*.

---

### **Truth**
*(Balade de Bon Conseyl)*

**I**
Flee fro the prees, and dwelle with sothfastnesse,
Suffyce unto thy good, though it be small;
For hord hath hate, and clymbyng tikelnesse,
Prees hath envye, and wele blent overal;
Savour no more than thee bihove shal;
Reule wel thyself, that other folk canst rede;
And trouthe shal delivere, it is no drede.

**II**
Tempest thee noght al croked to redresse,
In trust of hire that turneth as a ball:
Gret reste stant in litel besynesse;
An eek be war to sporne ayeyns an nalle;
Stryve not, as doth the crokke with the walle.
Daunte thyself, that dauntest otheres dede;
And trouthe shal delivere, it is no drede.

**III**
That thee is sent, receyve in buxumnesse;
The wrastling for this world axeth a fall.
Her is non hoom, her nis but wyldernesse:
Forth, pilgrim, forth! Forth, beste, out of thy stall!
Know thy contree, look up, thank God of all;
Hold the hye wey, and lat thy gost thee lede;
And trouthe shal delivere, it is no drede.

**Envoy**
Therfore, thou Vache, leve thyn old wrecchednesse
Unto the world; leve be thy lustinesse;
Mynde thy soule, and look up to the grace
Of hym that al hath wrought of his goodnesse;
And for thy part, send daun thy besynesse,
Hold the hye wey, and lat thy gost thee lede,
And trouthe shal delivere, it is no drede.

---

### **A Brief Contextual Note:**
* **"Vache" in the Envoy:** The envoy is addressed specifically to Sir Philip de la Vache, Chaucer's friend and son-in-law to Sir Richard Stury. "Vache" is also a pun on the French word for "cow," tying back to line 18 ("Forth, beste, out of thy stall!").
* **"trouthe":** In Middle English, *trouthe* meant more than just factual accuracy; it encompassed integrity, fidelity, honor, and spiritual loyalty to God.
* **Refrain:** *"And trouthe shal delivere, it is no drede"* translates modernly to *"And truth shall deliver [you], there is no doubt."*
